headline: Election Rally Pulls Mortgage Rates Lower
tileReason: The daily 30-year average fell to 7.22% Wednesday as bonds rallied on Democrats' election wins and a steep drop in oil; this morning yields are holding near two-month lows.
takeaway:
Mortgage rates fell back to their lowest in about six weeks. The daily 30-year average dropped 0.08% to 7.22% on Wednesday. Freddie Mac's weekly survey still shows 7.24% from last week; its new reading comes out at 9 AM PT today.

Wednesday's drop came from the election and oil. With Democrats winning both the House and Senate, investors expect less new government borrowing, and oil plunged more than 8% (Brent settled near $94.60) on bets that political pressure to end the Iran war will grow. Cheaper oil eases inflation worries, so the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, closed near 4.89%, down about 0.06%.

Lenders passed the rally along. Every daily survey we track moved lower: Zillow's average fell to 7.04% and the Mortgage Research Center's to about 7.09%. A weaker-than-expected reading on service businesses Wednesday also helped.

This morning brought mixed news. Weekly jobless claims fell to 189,000, matching the lowest level since 1969 and below the roughly 196,000 forecast, a sign layoffs remain rare, and worker productivity grew a strong 3.6%. Oil bounced about 1.5%, with Brent back near $96. Even so, the 10-year yield is roughly steady at about 4.87% to 4.90%, near its lowest in about two months, which points to steady lender pricing today.

A December Fed hike is still the base case. Futures markets, where traders bet on Fed decisions, put the odds of a quarter-point hike on Dec 9 at about 77% to 83%, depending on the source and time. Sticky inflation and a sturdy job market are why.

Borrowers still have a cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat 2.22% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 3, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%, so there is room for mortgage rates to improve if markets stay calm.

Next big tests: Friday's October jobs report, where forecasters expect only about 59,000 to 65,000 new jobs, and the Nov 10 inflation report.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.afterLabel: Nov 4–5, after the election results and strong jobless-claims data
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via Capp Notes (Nov 4 close) and Trading Economics (Nov 5 morning)
fedOdds.note: Odds of a quarter-point hike at the Dec 9 meeting were about 85% right after the Oct 28 hold. Sources differ: CME FedWatch showed about 77% after Wednesday's election rally, while Trading Economics puts it at about 80% to 83% this morning. Either way, a hike is still seen as the most likely outcome.

drivers.title: Democrats win both chambers of Congress
drivers.text: Investors see a divided government as less likely to pass big new tax cuts or spending, which would mean less government borrowing and fewer new Treasury bonds to sell. Less supply supports bond prices, so the 10-year yield fell about 0.06% Wednesday to near 4.89%, and the daily mortgage average dropped 0.08% to 7.22%.

drivers.title: Oil plunges on hopes for an end to the Iran war
drivers.text: Brent crude fell more than 8% Wednesday to settle near $94.60, its lowest since late August, on bets that the election results will add pressure for diplomacy with Iran. Cheaper oil lowers fuel and shipping costs, easing inflation worries and pulling bond yields down. Oil bounced about 1.5% this morning to near $96, and one research firm cut its odds of an Iran deal, so this support could fade quickly.

drivers.title: Layoffs stay rare and productivity jumps
drivers.text: Jobless claims fell to 189,000 this morning, matching the lowest since 1969, and productivity grew 3.6% in the third quarter. A sturdy job market can keep wages and spending up, which makes a Fed hike more likely and keeps a floor under rates. Strong productivity helps on the other side, because it lets the economy grow without as much inflation.

drivers.title: December Fed hike still seen as likely
drivers.text: Futures put the odds of a quarter-point Fed hike on Dec 9 at roughly 77% to 83%. When investors expect higher short-term rates, longer-term rates, including mortgages, have a harder time falling. Friday's jobs report and the Nov 10 inflation report will shape those odds.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat 2.22% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 3, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: if markets calm down, there is room for mortgage rates to improve even if Treasury yields stay put.

outlook.basis: Still close to a coin flip, with a lean toward rates staying about where they are. Rates just fell to a six-week low, so some of the good news is already priced in. In borrowers' favor: the election result lowers worries about heavy new government borrowing, oil is well off its late-October highs, the 10-year yield is near a two-month low, and mortgage rates are unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.22% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Working against them: layoffs are near record lows, a December Fed hike is still seen as likely (about 77% to 83%), inflation is well above target, and oil is already bouncing on Iran headlines. Big swing events: Friday's jobs report, the Nov 10 CPI report, next week's Treasury bond sales and any news from Iran.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average fell to about 7.22% Wednesday, its lowest in about six weeks and down from roughly 7.5% in early October, after the election and a big drop in oil pushed bond yields lower. Friday's jobs report and next week's inflation report could move rates either way, so it's worth talking with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates have eased, which helps affordability at the margin, but buyers are still stretched above 7%. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates just dipped to a six-week low around 7.22% after the election and a plunge in oil; Friday's jobs report is the next big test.
